claim: RIG-I detects cytosolic viral RNA and requires a conformational change caused by both ATP and RNA binding to induce an active signaling state and to trigger an immune response.
source: The innate immune sensor retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) detects cytosolic viral RNA and requires a conformational change caused by both ATP and RNA binding to induce an active signaling state and to trigger an immune response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge about RIG-I function, supported by the citation to previous work (Lässig et al., 2015).

claim: ATP hydrolysis removes RIG-I from lower-affinity self-RNAs.
source: Previously, we showed that ATP hydrolysis removes RIG-I from lower-affinity self-RNAs (Lässig et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A mutation in a motif that slows down ATP hydrolysis causes the autoimmune disease Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS).
source: Previously, we showed that ATP hydrolysis removes RIG-I from lower-affinity self-RNAs (Lässig et al., 2015), revealing how ATP turnover helps RIG-I distinguish viral from self-RNA and explaining why a mutation in a motif that slows down ATP hydrolysis causes the autoimmune disease Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and represents an established finding.

claim: The SMS variant C268F is localized in the ATP-binding P-loop.
source: Here we show that a different, mechanistically unexplained SMS variant, C268F, which is localized in the ATP-binding P-loop
evidence: This is a structural observation that is later confirmed by crystallographic data in the manuscript.

claim: RIG-I C268F can signal independently of ATP but is still dependent on RNA.
source: Here we show that a different, mechanistically unexplained SMS variant, C268F, which is localized in the ATP-binding P-loop, can signal independently of ATP but is still dependent on RNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assays and binding studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of RIG-I C268F in complex with double-stranded RNA reveals that C268F helps induce a structural conformation in RIG-I that is similar to that induced by ATP.
source: The structure of RIG-I C268F in complex with double-stranded RNA reveals that C268F helps induce a structural conformation in RIG-I that is similar to that induced by ATP.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A mutation in a P-loop ATPase can induce a gain-of-function ATP state in the absence of ATP.
source: Our results uncover an unexpected mechanism to explain how a mutation in a P-loop ATPase can induce a gain-of-function ATP state in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RLRs (RIG-I, MDA5 and LGP2) are members of the Superfamily II (SF2) helicases/translocases.
source: RLRs (RIG-I, MDA5 and LGP2) are members of the so-called Superfamily II (SF2) helicases/translocases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RLR protein family classification.

claim: RLRs share a multi-domain architecture that consists of a central SF2 ATPase domain accompanied by two N-terminal tandem caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD, only in RIG-I and MDA5) and a C-terminal regulatory domain (CTD or RD).
source: They share a multi-domain architecture that consists of a central SF2 ATPase domain accompanied by two N-terminal tandem caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD, only in RIG-I and MDA5) and a C-terminal regulatory domain (CTD or RD) (Rawling and Pyle, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RLR protein architecture, supported by citation.

claim: The SF2 domain is built out of an N-terminal RecA-like domain (1A) and a C-terminal RecA-like domain (2A) that together form an ATP-binding pocket, as well as an insertion domain (domain 2B).
source: The SF2 domain itself is built out of an N-terminal RecA-like domain (1A) and a C-terminal RecA-like domain (2A) that together form an ATP-binding pocket, as well as an insertion domain (domain 2B).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the SF2 domain architecture.

claim: SF2 and RD are crucial for RNA-recognition of RLRs.
source: SF2 and RD are crucial for RNA-recognition of RLRs, whereas 2CARD communicates successful RNA-binding events to downstream signaling factors (Jiang et al., 2011; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: 2CARD communicates successful RNA-binding events to downstream signaling factors.
source: SF2 and RD are crucial for RNA-recognition of RLRs, whereas 2CARD communicates successful RNA-binding events to downstream signaling factors (Jiang et al., 2011; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on RLR signaling mechanisms.

claim: RIG-I detects dsRNA ends harbouring 5' tri- or diphosphates.
source: Specifically, RIG-I detects dsRNA ends harbouring 5' tri- or diphosphates (Goubau et al., 2014; Schlee et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RIG-I ligand specificity, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Simultaneous binding of an RNA ligand and ATP to RIG-I switches the protein into an active state in which the otherwise shielded 2CARD is released.
source: Simultaneous binding of an RNA ligand and ATP to RIG-I switches the protein into an active state in which the otherwise shielded 2CARD is released (Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: Activated RIG-I homo-tetramerizes via 2CARD.
source: Activated RIG-I homo-tetramerizes via 2CARD (Jiang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: Activated RIG-I nucleates the polymerisation of its adapter protein, mitochondrial antiviral-signaling (MAVS), to elicit the innate immune signaling cascade.
source: Activated RIG-I homo-tetramerizes via 2CARD (Jiang et al., 2012) and nucleates the polymerisation of its adapter protein, mitochondrial antiviral-signaling (MAVS), to elicit the innate immune signaling cascade (Peisley et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on RIG-I signaling mechanisms.

claim: Self-ribonucleic acids are shielded from RLRs by introducing 2'O-methylations or by destabilizing double-stranded parts through A-to-I editing.
source: Self-ribonucleic acids for instance are shielded from RLRs by introducing 2'O-methylations or by destabilizing double-stranded parts through A-to-I editing (Chung et al., 2018; Devarkar et al., 2016; Liddicoat et al., 2015; Schuberth-Wagner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on self-RNA discrimination mechanisms.

claim: The SF2 domain of RLRs confers a proof-reading activity by removing RIG-I from self-RNA to avoid autoimmunity.
source: In addition, we and others have been able to show that the SF2 domain of RLRs itself confers a proof-reading activity by removing RIG-I from self-RNA so as to avoid autoimmunity (Anchisi et al., 2015; Lässig et al., 2015; Louber et al., 2015; Rawling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the authors' previous work.

claim: ATP turnover can lead to translocation on dsRNA stems that could remove the protein from the RNA and reinstall the inactivated state.
source: In particular, ATP turnover can lead to translocation on dsRNA stems that could remove the protein from the RNA and reinstall the inactivated state (Myong et al., 2009; Yao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on RIG-I dynamics.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause system-wide autoimmune diseases such as Aicardi-Goutière syndrome (AGS).
source: For instance, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause system-wide autoimmune diseases such as Aicardi-Goutière syndrome (AGS) (Oda et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS).
source: For instance, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause system-wide autoimmune diseases such as Aicardi-Goutière syndrome (AGS) (Oda et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2014), Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) (Jang et al., 2015; Rutsch et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: For instance, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause system-wide autoimmune diseases such as Aicardi-Goutière syndrome (AGS) (Oda et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2014), Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) (Jang et al., 2015; Rutsch et al., 2015), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Cunninghame Graham et al., 2011; Pettersson et al., 2017; Van Eyck et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause type 1 diabetes.
source: For instance, single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RLR genes are known to cause system-wide autoimmune diseases such as Aicardi-Goutière syndrome (AGS) (Oda et al., 2014; Rice et al., 2014), Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) (Jang et al., 2015; Rutsch et al., 2015), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Cunninghame Graham et al., 2011; Pettersson et al., 2017; Van Eyck et al., 2015) or type 1 diabetes (Liu et al., 2009; Smyth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: The RIG-I SMS variants C268F and E373A are located within SF2 ATP binding and hydrolysis motifs I and II, respectively.
source: The RIG-I SMS variants C268F and E373A are located within SF2 ATP binding and hydrolysis motifs I and II, respectively, (Fairman-Williams et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by citation and structural data shown in the figure.

claim: RIG-I SMS variants C268F and E373A were previously shown to be constitutively active in reporter cells without any external dsRNA trigger.
source: The RIG-I SMS variants C268F and E373A are located within SF2 ATP binding and hydrolysis motifs I and II, respectively, (Fairman-Williams et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and were previously shown to be constitutively active in reporter cells without any external dsRNA trigger (Jang et al., 2015; Lässig et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in the figure.

claim: RIG-I E373A's enhanced immune signaling ability can be explained by proficient ATP binding but reduced ATP hydrolysis.
source: RIG-I E373A's enhanced immune signaling ability can be explained by proficient ATP binding but reduced ATP hydrolysis, since the motif II glutamate is implicated in positioning and polarizing the attacking water molecule in the hydrolysis reaction.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the role of motif II glutamate in ATP hydrolysis and previous experimental data.

claim: The motif II glutamate is implicated in positioning and polarizing the attacking water molecule in the hydrolysis reaction.
source: RIG-I E373A's enhanced immune signaling ability can be explained by proficient ATP binding but reduced ATP hydrolysis, since the motif II glutamate is implicated in positioning and polarizing the attacking water molecule in the hydrolysis reaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the catalytic mechanism of ATPases.

claim: The stabilized ATP state in RIG-I E373A leads to increased binding of and activation by endogenous dsRNA.
source: The stabilized ATP state leads to increased binding of and activation by endogenous dsRNA (Lässig et al., 2015; Louber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RIG-I mutant K270A possesses reduced ATP binding properties.
source: For instance, a designed and widely used mutant with a defect in the invariant ATP phosphate-binding motif I lysine, K270A, possesses reduced ATP binding properties (Rawling et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The RIG-I K270A/I mutant is deficient in inducing an immune response.
source: For instance, a designed and widely used mutant with a defect in the invariant ATP phosphate-binding motif I lysine, K270A, possesses reduced ATP binding properties (Rawling et al., 2015) and the RIG-I K270A/I mutant is deficient in inducing an immune response (Lässig et al., 2015; Yoneyama et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The RIG-I SMS variant C268F is constitutively active.
source: By contrast, the RIG-I SMS variant C268F shows the opposite effect and is constitutively active, although this mutation is only two amino acids away from K270A in the same ATP phosphate-binding 'P-loop' in motif I (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: RIG-I C268F, T347A fails to induce the IFN-β promoter in uninfected as well as in 19mer 5'-triphosphate (ppp)-dsRNA-stimulated cells.
source: Our assays show, that RIG-I C268F, T347A fails to induce the IFN-β promoter in uninfected as well as in 19mer 5'-triphosphate (ppp)-dsRNA-stimulated cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from luciferase reporter assays presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The RIG-I SMS single-mutant C268F induces immune signaling only if bound to endogenous or transfected RNA.
source: Our assays show, that RIG-I C268F, T347A fails to induce the IFN-β promoter in uninfected as well as in 19mer 5'-triphosphate (ppp)-dsRNA-stimulated cells, indicating that the RIG-I SMS single-mutant C268F induces immune signaling only if bound to endogenous or transfected RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the double mutant with impaired RNA binding cannot signal.

claim: Competition assays of RIG-I C268F titrated with signaling-deficient RIG-I lacking the 2CARD domain (RIG-I Δ2CARD) or with RIG-I Δ2CARD E373Q gradually decreased the IFN-β promoter-driven luciferase activity.
source: In addition, competition assays of RIG-I C268F titrated with signaling-deficient RIG-I lacking the 2CARD domain (RIG-I Δ2CARD) or with RIG-I Δ2CARD E373Q also gradually decreased the IFN-β promoter-driven luciferase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: RIG-I C268F and RIG-I Δ2CARD (E373Q) recognize identical RNA substrates.
source: Thus, RIG-I C268F as well as RIG-I Δ2CARD (E373Q) seem to recognize identical RNA substrates which are, however, saturated with signaling-deficient RIG-I Δ2CARD (E373Q) at higher transfected DNA concentrations thus preventing an immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition assay data.

claim: The RIG-I C268F SMS mutation does not lead to a liberation of the 2CARD signaling module in the absence of RNA.
source: Furthermore, we can exclude the possibility that the RIG-I C268F SMS mutation leads to a liberation of the 2CARD signaling module in the absence of RNA, for example by unfolding SF2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing RNA-dependence of signaling.

claim: Signaling by the RIG-I C268F SMS variant is dependent on 2CARD release triggered by binding to RNA molecules.
source: Instead, signaling by the RIG-I C268F SMS variant is dependent on 2CARD release triggered by binding to RNA molecules, as it is in wild type RIG-I.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing RNA-dependence of signaling.

claim: Wild type RIG-I shows a moderate binding affinity to hpRNA that is further decreased in the presence of ATP.
source: As expected, wild type RIG-I shows a moderate binding affinity to this ligand that is further decreased in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RIG-I C268F displays an increased affinity to hpRNA that is even enhanced in the presence of ATP.
source: By contrast, RIG-I C268F displays an already increased affinity to the hpRNA that is even enhanced in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RIG-I C268F has increased co-purification with endogenous RNA molecules.
source: This confirms the previous results for RIG-I C268F showing an increased co-purification with endogenous RNA molecules (Lässig et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RIG-I C268F has two conformations (apo and ATP-bound) that have increased dsRNA affinity.
source: This confirms the previous results for RIG-I C268F showing an increased co-purification with endogenous RNA molecules (Lässig et al., 2015) and indicates that RIG-I C268F has two conformations (apo and ATP-bound) that have increased dsRNA affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding data showing increased affinity in both presence and absence of ATP.

claim: ATP hydrolysis assays with 32P-labeled ATP confirmed a loss of catalytic activity of RIG-I C268F in the presence of dsRNA.
source: ATP hydrolysis assays with 32P-labeled ATP confirmed a loss of catalytic activity of RIG-I C268F and of both motif I and II mutants in the presence of dsRNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RIG-I C268F has defects in dissociating from endogenous RNA because it lacks the capability for ATP turnover and hence translocation.
source: In accordance with our RNA-binding experiments, this evidence supports a model in which RIG-I C268F has defects in dissociating from endogenous RNA, because it lacks the capability for ATP turnover and hence translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATP hydrolysis and RNA binding data.

claim: Wild type RIG-I and ATP-hydrolysis-deficient RIG-I E373Q show comparable affinities for MANT-ATP and MANT-ATPγS in the low µM range in the absence of any RNA ligand.
source: In the absence of any RNA ligand, both wild type RIG-I and ATP-hydrolysis-deficient RIG-I E373Q show comparable affinities for MANT-ATP and MANT-ATPγS in the low µM range (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: ATP-binding-deficient RIG-I K270I has a reduced affinity for ATP in the medium µM range.
source: As expected, ATP-binding-deficient RIG-I K270I has a reduced affinity for ATP (in the medium µM range).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The presence of RNA increases the affinity of wtRIG-I and RIG-I E373Q for MANT-ATP or MANT-ATPγS.
source: In accordance with previous data (Kohlway et al., 2013), the presence of RNA increases the affinity of wtRIG-I and RIG-I E373Q, but not of RIG-I K270I for MANT-ATP or MANT-ATPγS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of RNA does not increase the affinity of RIG-I K270I for MANT-ATP or MANT-ATPγS.
source: In accordance with previous data (Kohlway et al., 2013), the presence of RNA increases the affinity of wtRIG-I and RIG-I E373Q, but not of RIG-I K270I for MANT-ATP or MANT-ATPγS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The RIG-I SMS variant C268F displays reduced ATP-binding affinities compared to that of wtRIG-I or RIG-I E373Q independently of the availability of an RNA ligand.
source: Interestingly, like RIG-I K270I, the RIG-I SMS variant C268F displays reduced ATP-binding affinities compared to that of wtRIG-I or RIG-I E373Q independently of the availability of an RNA ligand (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Both RNA and ATP binding are normally needed to induce a molecular switch within RIG-I in order to release the 2CARD module and to activate an immune response.
source: This is puzzling as both RNA and ATP binding are normally needed to induce a molecular switch within RIG-I in order to release the 2CARD module and to activate an immune response (Shah et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RIG-I C268F might be able to signal even in the absence of a bound ATP molecule.
source: RIG-I C268F might thus be able to signal even in the absence of a bound ATP molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced ATP binding but maintained signaling activity.

claim: The molecular switch to release 2CARD is only triggered in RIG-I C268F but not in RIG-I K270I.
source: However, even though it is possible that under cellular conditions of 1 mM ATP or even higher, ATP is still bound by both motif I mutants, the molecular switch to release 2CARD is only triggered in RIG-I C268F but not in RIG-I K270I (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The SMS mutant RIG-I C268F shows crucial amino acid side chain rearrangements in the active site that stabilize the protein in an activated state but prevent binding and co-crystalization of a nucleotide.
source: Intriguingly, despite an overall high structural similarity to wtRIG-I Δ2CARD bound to dsRNA (Jiang et al., 2011), the SMS mutant shows crucial amino acid side chain rearrangements in the active site that stabilize the protein in an activated state but prevent binding and co-crystalization of a nucleotide (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data shown in the figures.

claim: The bulky F268 side chain displaces the evolutionary invariant motif I K270 from its central ATP phosphate-binding position in the P-loop, into a position where the Nε of K270 is situated at a site normally occupied by the Mg2+ ion.
source: In particular, the bulky F268 side chain displaces the evolutionary invariant motif I K270 from its central ATP phosphate-binding position in the P-loop, into a position where the Nε of K270 is situated at a site normally occupied by the Mg2+ ion (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data shown in the video and figures.

claim: K270 forms a salt bridge with E702 from the C-terminal RecA-like domain 2A in RIG-I C268F.
source: As a result, K270 now forms a salt bridge with E702 from the C-terminal RecA-like domain 2A, which in turn occupies the ATP γ-phosphate binding site.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data.

claim: E702 occupies the ATP γ-phosphate binding site in RIG-I C268F.
source: As a result, K270 now forms a salt bridge with E702 from the C-terminal RecA-like domain 2A, which in turn occupies the ATP γ-phosphate binding site.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data.

claim: The overall conformation of RIG-I C268F resembles the ATP-bound state of RIG-I, but without ATP.
source: The resulting overall conformation resembles the ATP-bound state of RIG-I, but without ATP, and could thus explain how C268F is able to signal independently of any nucleotide.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic structural data and comparison with wild-type structures.

claim: Mutation of K270 in RecA-like domain A1 renders RIG-I C268F inactive.
source: Indeed, mutation of K270 in RecA-like domain A1 renders RIG-I C268F inactive, probably as the result of a mixture of (i) prevention of the activation of RIG-I C268F in the absence of ATP by disrupting the salt bridge, and/or (ii) the failure to bind ATP altogether through impaired ATP phosphate coordination and thus an impaired 2CARD release.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutation of E702 in the RecA-like domain 2A of RIG-I C268F does not disrupt constitutive signaling of the protein, although this activity is at a reduced level compared to that of RIG-I C268F.
source: Mutation of E702 in the RecA-like domain 2A of RIG-I C268F, by contrast, does not disrupt constitutive signaling of the protein, although this activity is at a reduced level compared to that of RIG-I C268F.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: E702A alone already induces an autoimmune phenotype similar to that induced by RIG-I C268F, E702A.
source: Similar to our previously described V699A mutant in the same motif (Lässig et al., 2015), E702A alone already induces an autoimmune phenotype similar to that induced by RIG-I C268F, E702A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: RIG-I C268F stabilizes an ATP-like state in the absence of ATP, but still allows formation of a proper ATP-bound state.
source: The most plausible explanation for these data is that RIG-I C268F stabilizes an ATP-like state in the absence of ATP, but still allows formation of a proper ATP-bound state.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: ATP further increases the binding of RIG-I C268F to internal dsRNA stems.
source: However, our data also show that ATP further increases the binding of RIG-I C268F to internal dsRNA stems (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Engineering of ATP-binding mutations R244A, Q247A into RIG-I C268F at least partly reduces its signaling activity in response to endogenous or ppp-dsRNA RNA.
source: However, our data also show that ATP further increases the binding of RIG-I C268F to internal dsRNA stems (Figure 1B) and that the engineering of ATP-binding mutations R244A, Q247A into RIG-I C268F at least partly reduces its signaling activity in response to endogenous or ppp-dsRNA RNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Binding of ATP at high molecular concentrations, such as those present in a cellular context, further contributes to the pathogenic signaling activity of RIG-I C268F.
source: Even though we were not able to co-crystalize RIG-I C268F in the presence of a nucleotide, it is very possible that binding of ATP at high molecular concentrations, such as those present in a cellular context, further contributes to the pathogenic signaling activity of the protein.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism unifies the molecular basis for the development of SMS by both RIG-I variants C268F and E373A.
source: This mechanism unifies the molecular basis for the development of SMS by both RIG-I variants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and structural data presented.

claim: Wild type RIG-I consumes ATP and uses ATP turnover to decrease its affinity to self-RNA.
source: Unlike wtRIG-I, which consumes ATP and uses ATP turnover to decrease its affinity to self-RNA (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by previous work and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Both motif I and II SMS mutations either mimic or freeze RIG-I in an ATP-bound state.
source: Unlike wtRIG-I, which consumes ATP and uses ATP turnover to decrease its affinity to self-RNA (Figure 4A), both motif I and II SMS mutations either mimic or freeze RIG-I in an ATP-bound state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and structural data presented.

claim: The inability to hydrolyze ATP and thus to dissociate actively from RNA traps RIG-I SMS variants in an activated state and thus explains autoimmune signaling in response to self-RNA.
source: As a consequence, the inability to hydrolyze ATP and thus to dissociate actively from RNA (Figure 1B, Figure 2A) traps the protein in an activated state and thus explains autoimmune signaling in response to self-RNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Slight intramolecular rearrangements within the RIG-I C268F ATP-binding pocket appear to compensate for ATP binding and render the protein active in the presence of dsRNA only.
source: Slight intramolecular rearrangements within the RIG-I C268F ATP-binding pocket appear to compensate for ATP binding and render the protein active in the presence of dsRNA only.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Loss of proof-reading activity in RIG-I C268F leads to increased activation by endogenous RNA.
source: At the same time, loss of proof-reading activity leads to increased activation by endogenous RNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing loss of ATP hydrolysis and increased RNA binding.

claim: A P-loop mutation can mimic the effects of ATP binding.
source: This unusual gain-of-function mutation reveals, for the first time to our knowledge, that a P-loop mutation can mimic the effects of ATP binding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Crystal 1 had space group P212121 and diffracted to 3.3 Å.
source: Crystal 1 had space group P212121 and diffracted to 3.3 Å, crystal 2 had space group P6522 and diffracted until 2.9 Å (Table 2).
evidence: This is crystallographic data reported in the methods section.

claim: Crystal 2 had space group P6522 and diffracted until 2.9 Å.
source: Crystal 1 had space group P212121 and diffracted to 3.3 Å, crystal 2 had space group P6522 and diffracted until 2.9 Å (Table 2).
evidence: This is crystallographic data reported in the methods section.

claim: No density for a bound nucleotide was detected in either structure of RIG-I C268F.
source: We did not detect any density for a bound nucleotide in either structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the crystallographic data analysis.

claim: T347A point mutation in the RNA-binding interface of the N-terminal RecA-like domain (1A) abrogates the signaling of wild type RIG-I in infected cells.
source: In particular, we used a previously described T347A point mutation in the RNA-binding interface of the N-terminal RecA-like domain (1A) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), that abrogates the signaling of wild type (wt) RIG-I in infected cells and decreases the affinity for dsRNA in vitro (Lässig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: T347A point mutation decreases the affinity for dsRNA in vitro.
source: In particular, we used a previously described T347A point mutation in the RNA-binding interface of the N-terminal RecA-like domain (1A) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), that abrogates the signaling of wild type (wt) RIG-I in infected cells and decreases the affinity for dsRNA in vitro (Lässig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RIG-I has an affinity for MANT-ATP of 72 ± 13 µM.
source: RIG-I 72 ± 13 µM
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: RIG-I E373Q has an affinity for MANT-ATP of 72 ± 13 µM.
source: RIG-I E373Q 72 ± 13 µM
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: RIG-I E373Q in the presence of RNA has an affinity for MANT-ATP of 28 ± 5 µM.
source: RIG-I E373Q + RNA 28 ± 5 µM
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: RIG-I K270I has an affinity for MANT-ATP of 298 ± 81 µM.
source: RIG-I K270I 298 ± 81 µM
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: RIG-I C268F has an affinity for MANT-ATP of 166 ± 34 µM.
source: RIG-I C268F 166 ± 34 µM
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 1.
